start-here-demo-1-with-your-own-wallet-a.text: Start here: Demo 1 with your own wallet and Koios.

As a Cardano developer who knows cardano-cli, wallets, faucets and Koios but has never used Singular, you want to run Demo 1 yourself: create a registry, put keys in it, change them, end them, and see every refusal appear where the documentation says it will. You use a Koios API you choose and a wallet whose signing key stays sealed in a vault on your machine, or on the machine that signs. Commands read and submit through Koios, take their time from a pinned recording, and build and evaluate everything locally. They do not need a node socket.
Two pages carry you from the first command to the last, and both can be copied as they stand:
The rest of this page explains the settings, the signing choices and the limits of what a command's answers prove.

download-and-check-the-release.text: Releases are listed at https://github.com/lambdasistemi/singular/releases, and the newest is at https://github.com/lambdasistemi/singular/releases/latest. A release carries three files: the on-chain archive singular-onchain-X.Y.Z.tar.gz (the compiled validators, the sources of both commands and the run page), the documentation archive singular-docs-X.Y.Z.tar.gz (220 MB, not needed to play Demo 1) and SHA256SUMS for both. The file names carry the version without a v, and the archive extracts into the current directory, so extract it into a directory of its own. The exact commands, with the checks, are on Play Demo 1 on preprod.

The quickest way to the programs is the Nix shell of singular-demo. nix develop github:lambdasistemi/singular-demo --accept-flake-config opens a shell with singular, open-datum, the development node devnet and jq already built by the project's CI, and fetches about 190 MiB from the public caches instead of compiling anything. Its limits: it is pinned to release v0.12.0, it is built for x86_64 Linux only, it needs Nix, and it keeps the development node's files in one directory per user, so run one node at a time. On a multi-user Nix install a user who is not in trusted-users cannot take the caches from a flake; that repository's README says what to change. You still need the archive, for the run page, the blueprint and the readback script. The shell's own $blueprint holds the same bytes as the archive's onchain/plutus.json, but it sits in the Nix store with no version.txt beside it, which singular registry describe refuses without, so name the archive's file as the blueprint.

The second route builds the two commands from the archive itself. It suits another release or another system. It compiles a large Haskell stack unless the project's public binary cache serves it, and the runbook says how. No release ships ready-built binaries yet. A binary install that needs no Nix is coming in issue 695.

choose-the-network-and-api.text: Your commands read the chain and send signed transactions through the API you choose. The project's own private development chain sits behind an HTTP facade that speaks the same dialect as Koios; your commands name your API instead.

The generated development network's magic is 42, and its launcher supplies its exact published time directory. A supplied directory contains time-manifest.json, shelley-genesis.json and era-history.cbor; their raw identities, network, system start and protocol-major pin are validated. Unsupported time networks refuse rather than borrowing another recording. Writes refuse mainnet.
The old --backend and --node-socket settings are refused on every command. A socket accepted by a separate private probe is a setting of the project's own test tools, not an ordinary provider route.

make-a-wallet-and-fund-it.text: Make a wallet and fund it.

Make a wallet with singular wallet create, giving --network-magic 1 for preprod. It seals a fresh signing key in an encrypted vault and prints the wallet's address. At a terminal it asks for the passphrase twice, an entry and a confirmation, and refuses a confirmation that differs; in a script, --passphrase-fd FD supplies it as one line read once. singular wallet address asks once, and prints the same address again from the vault.

Fund that address from the preprod faucet. One ada-only output is enough: nothing is split and no self-payment is needed, because every write spends the wallet's largest ada-only output and returns its change. What a play costs, as measured on preprod on 18 October 2026: thirteen registry transactions came to 6.92 tADA in fees; each waiting request holds 3 tADA (the key's 2 tADA deposit and a 1 tADA folder's fee); each active key keeps its 2 tADA deposit until it is terminated; and creating a registry needs at least 162.65 tADA when no script of the release is on chain yet, a figure measured on a development node. The runbook has the table. A command that finds the wallet short refuses before it submits, naming the shortfall. A key's bytes do not belong in command output or receipts.

sign-each-write.text: Each write takes exactly one signer. Your own open-datum and singular registry commands sign in one of two ways.
From your vault: add --vault FILE, and --passphrase-fd FD in a script. The command opens the vault once, builds the run, signs it in memory and sends it.

Elsewhere: name the wallet's address with --wallet-address ADDR and a new bundle file with --bundle FILE. The command writes its transactions there and exits with status 19, waiting-for-signatures. Sign the bundle with singular wallet sign --vault FILE and send it with singular submit.

The settings table in the command reference lists the flags of each way, and the development-node page shows both ways from the first command to the last. Key files are not a way to start: they remain on a few harness commands until the project retires them (issue 672).

how-a-write-is-confirmed.text: A successful submission answer alone is not confirmation. Confirmation requires the exact output. With a validity upper bound the provider deadline is that slot's POSIX start plus 120 seconds; without one it is now plus 300 seconds. Latest-block observation can establish expiry. A refusal, unavailable answer, timeout or mismatching proof stops the run; it is never counted as its intended accepting step.

what-a-providers-answers-do-and-do-not-p.text: What a provider's answers do and do not prove.

A command reads several facts through one logical session. The session is called unbound: its reads may observe different chain states, so nothing promises one coherent snapshot. Facts are called unverified: no configured witness checks that the API answered honestly. Raw-source receipts identify what was consumed; they do not prove the API answered honestly or that all reads were a coherent snapshot. Ledger acceptance remains an independent boundary.

Before construction, the builder selects an interval with at least ten seconds of usable slots at its observed tip. The moving ledger horizon can shorten the upper bound. An empty interval refuses WindowPastLedgerHorizon; a nonempty registry-limited short interval refuses WindowTooShort. Only a horizon-limited otherwise longer window permits one wait for a later horizon, bounded by slots and 20 seconds of wall time. A stalled wait refuses HorizonWaitTimedOut before signing. Build duration can consume the selected interval; this rule is not a guarantee of eventual ledger acceptance.

what-is-delivered-and-what-is-not.text: What is delivered and what is not.

Demo 1 has two users, Alice and Bob, who start with empty homes. Neither creates the registry for the other or receives its creation files. Each joins with the registry's state token, their own wallet and a Koios URL, with no shared directory: every command carries --state-token and no directory option, and neither user opens the other's files. Each can also read the registry page generated from the chain: which registry this is, which release it runs, what its rules are and what it holds, from the token and the packaged release alone. Joining by a copied identity file is superseded.

Not delivered: a block anchor for the last fold, documentation links checked against a published asset, and the independently derived action identity in the public report. Public replay reconstructs the registry's trie; missing history or a root that does not chain remains a named refusal. Historical deployment and naming receipts remain evidence of their recorded revision and public chain, not a pass for this provider candidate.

The bounded registry journey and the deployment tool are run by the project for now. They keep key files until issue 672 gives them a vault, and this page does not teach them. No required hosted workflow currently exercises the legacy deployment-attach script, so attached naming is not claimed runnable. The retained register-rows, recovery-rows and retirement-rows commands remain unverified under #172 and #283. The recovery and retirement guide documents that design, and the preprod record preserves its historical executed values.
